passages.original: interioris autem loci præcipua semper ac perpetua dignitas ;non quia dexter aut sinister, sed quia superior, quia prior, quia medius quodammodo : medius, inquam, inter comitem, et illud quidquid est quod nlterum latus claudit. Sic enim Græci μέσυν ἔχειν, μέσον λοξείν, etiam de duobus dicunt, cum alter interiore loco recipitur : ut Plutarchus in Catone Uticeusi, quem ait Philostrato, cum una deamholarent, exteriorem incessisse ob honorem philosophiæ. ϕιλοσοϕίας,et vetus interpres Juvenalis versum exponens sutyræ 3 : Div ilis hic servi claudit tatus ingenuorum Filius. Aut in medium, inquit, servum mittit, autin sinistra ambulat. Quibus verbis totam praterea sententiam nostram mirifice confirmat. De duobus enim sermo est, ut apud Horatium, cujus umbra hoc loco Juven alis. Quare duo hæcita distigut, ut in medium mttere s i interi rem I: cum dare, sive læva sive dextra , in sinistra ambulare, tum scilicet quando neuter locus interior esi.
passages.english: But the inner place always had a special and lasting dignity, not because it was on the right or the left, but because it was higher, because it was first, because it was in some way in the middle: in the middle, I say, between the companion and whatever it is that closes off the other side. For thus the Greeks say *meson echein* ["to hold the middle"] and *meson lambanein* ["to take the middle"] even of two people, when one is received into the inner place. So Plutarch in his *Cato of Utica* says that Cato, when he walked about together with Philostratus, went on the outer side out of honour for philosophy. And the old commentator on Juvenal, explaining the line of the third satire, "Here the son of freeborn parents closes the side of a rich man's slave," says: "Either he puts the slave in the middle, or he walks on the left." With these words he moreover confirms our whole view remarkably well. For the talk is of two people, as in Horace, whom Juvenal echoes in this passage. Therefore he distinguishes these two things thus: to put [someone] in the middle is to give [him] the inner place, whether on the left or on the right; to walk on the left [applies] precisely when neither place is the inner one.
passages.notes: The Greek is garbled by the scan: "μέσυν ἔχειν, μέσον λοξείν" is read as μέσον ἔχειν and μέσον λαμβάνειν (the second is a conjecture). A stray "ϕιλοσοϕίας" after "philosophiæ" appears to be a fragment of the Greek quotation from Plutarch and is not translated separately. Many scanning errors corrected: "nlterum" (alterum), "Uticeusi" (Uticensi), "deamholarent" (deambularent), "sutyræ" (satyrae), "Div ilis" (Divitis), "tatus" (latus), "autin" (aut in), "praterea" (praeterea). The final sentence is badly corrupted ("hæcita distigut, ut in medium mttere s i interi rem I: cum dare"); read as "haec ita distinguit, ut in medium mittere sit interiorem locum dare". The Juvenal line is Sat. 3.131–132.
